title: No Trace in Any Log: How Meta Hunts Silent Data Corruption
summary: A silent data corruption is a hardware error that nothing notices: a defective chip computes a wrong answer and reports no error, writes no log line, trips no alert. The bad result simply flows downstream, spreads across services, and surfaces weeks later as an application bug with no trace pointing back to the chip that caused it. And the defect is hard to catch at the source: a CPU gets a few hours of testing at the vendor and a couple of days at the integrator, then runs in the fleet for years, where its defects worsen with age and heat. Harish Dixit's post describes Meta's answer, drawn from 3+ years in production: since no passive signal can ever reveal the failure, you have to manufacture the evidence. You ask each machine questions whose answers you already know, and treat a wrong answer as the only symptom you will ever get. Meta does this at two depths: a deep test that runs during maintenance windows, and a shallow test that runs constantly beside live workloads. Its central finding is that a fleet needs both.
crux: A silent data corruption is a gray failure at the silicon level: the machine is neither up nor down, it is wrong. A defect in circuitry that has no check logic doesn't crash the machine or slow it; it makes the machine compute a wrong answer and report success, leaving no record or trace in any system log. Every health signal the fleet collects answers a different question, is the machine up and responsive and cool, than the one that matters: is the machine telling the truth? No passive signal can answer that. So the conclusion is forced: if observation can never reveal the failure, the evidence has to be manufactured. You ask the hardware questions whose answers you already know and treat a wrong answer as the only trustworthy symptom that will ever exist — done at two depths, briefly and constantly beside live workloads, deeply and rarely during maintenance. Two other systems in behindscale hit the same invisible-failure wall: Slack, where components were neither healthy nor dead, and Cloudflare, where machines lied mid-incident. Meta meets it at its purest, in silicon.
cruxSummary: Defective silicon computes wrong answers and leaves no record in any log.
problem:
The post's definition is the problem statement. A silent data corruption damages the correctness of a computation, and its causes are physical: the way data flows through specific circuits, temperature swings, and the chip's age, among other silicon factors. It leaves no record or trace in any system log. It stays hidden inside a workload and spreads across several services, so the damage shows up in systems far from the defective part — data loss and application-level bugs that can take months to debug once a corruption's residue has spread through the software. With no way to detect it early, an application can be exposed for months.

The manufacturing pipeline explains why the fleet inherits the problem. A server or CPU is tested for a few hours at the vendor, a couple of days at the integrator in the best case, and only on a sampling basis after that. Then the part enters a production fleet of enormous scale, where testing is genuinely hard. Every test takes time away from production work; testing a machine that is out of production pays a cost to ramp down and back up around each run; testing a machine still in production risks leaving behind settings that hurt its performance. Across a whole fleet, both the variation between machines and the total time add up. Meta frames the two challenges as a pair: for in-production testing, share the machine politely with minimal effect on the workload; for out-of-production testing, use the downtime a machine already has without disturbing the maintenance that created it.

What makes the failure gray rather than merely rare is the dead end it creates for observation: there is no log line to alert on, no error counter to graph, no health check that a lying CPU fails. Detection cannot be observed into existence. It has to be manufactured.
solution:
Meta's answer is to actively interrogate the hardware at two depths, and the post's conclusion is that both matter equally: deploy both in any large fleet.

The deep test (Meta calls its tool Fleetscanner) piggybacks on the maintenance events machines already go through: reboots, kernel and firmware upgrades, reimages, provisioning, and repairs. Because the machine is already out of production, the test can run for minutes and be as intrusive as it needs to be, which a live machine could never tolerate. Its weakness is its schedule, and the post is honest about it: given how often machines cycle through maintenance, a given machine gets tested about once every 180 days (sensitive tiers can be set to test more often). A corruption that arrives just after a test can operate for months before the next one. The cost is honest too: most maintenance now takes longer by the length of a test, so test time and frequency are weighed carefully against how much they actually catch. The running total: more than 68 million tests and roughly 4 billion machine-seconds of testing (cumulative test time added up across the fleet), all harvested from downtime that already existed.

The shallow test (Meta's tool is Ripple) exists because the deep test structurally cannot catch three things: corruptions that arrive between maintenance windows, corruptions that only appear for particular data patterns the deep test never tried, and corruptions triggered when the chip switches between operating modes. The shallow test runs alongside the live workload, injecting bit patterns with known correct answers on a set per-service schedule, with fine controls over how often, how long, and on what hardware it runs. Each run is about 1,000× shorter than a deep test: hundreds of milliseconds. Its constantly refreshed test values and deliberately triggered mode-switches catch defects that only show up across thousands of repetitions. The cost to the workload is real but measured as negligible next to ordinary fleet management, and Meta's early results were shared with CPU vendors, who built similar checks into their own tools. The scale: about 2.5 billion unique tests and seeds per month, and nearly 100 million seconds of testing run beside live work.

The coverage comparison is the argument for running both. The shallow test reaches 70% of corruption coverage in about 15 days; the deep test takes roughly 6 months to reach the same point. But 23% of faulty CPUs are found only by the deep test, and another 7% only by the shallow test running long enough to accumulate repetitions. Fast-and-shallow finds most defects quickly; slow-and-deep finds the ones nothing else ever will. The split is expected to shift by defect type, so Meta keeps revisiting it to tune what each test checks, how often, and for how long. The closing stance treats the problem as permanent infrastructure: applications are too sensitive to corruption, and the exposure windows too costly, for detection to be anything but an always-on priority.
tradeoffs: Health signals answer the wrong question. Liveness, responsiveness, thermals, error counters: every passive signal the fleet collects assumes a failure will announce itself, and silent corruption's defining trait is that it doesn't. No record, no trace, no log line. This is the class lesson at its purest. When a failure is invisible to the system's own signals, adding more monitoring of the same kind catches nothing new. The only question worth asking, "is this machine telling the truth?", can be answered only by asking questions whose answers you already know.

Vendor testing lasts hours; a chip runs for years. A few hours at the vendor, a couple of days at the integrator, sampling after that, against silicon whose defects worsen with age and heat over years of service. The gap between how much a chip is tested at manufacture and how long its defects take to emerge is structural, which is why detection had to become a job the fleet does continuously rather than a box the supplier checks once. It is also why Meta feeding results back to CPU vendors closed a loop the industry didn't previously have.

The deep test rides on downtime you already paid for. Piggybacking minutes-long, intrusive tests onto reboots, upgrades, and repairs turns existing maintenance into detection at almost no extra cost. The catch is twofold: every maintenance event now runs longer by one test, and the schedule is hostage to how often machines cycle. About once every 180 days per machine means a defect can own a machine for half a year between deep looks. The deep test is cheap precisely because it doesn't control its own timing.

The constant test has to interfere as little as possible with the real work it runs beside. Because it lives on the same machines as live production workloads, everything about it is kept small and controllable: runs of a few hundred milliseconds, per-service schedules, per-workload on/off switches, hardware controls, and a footprint measured as negligible. Keeping it that unobtrusive is what buys the coverage the deep test can't: corruptions that arrive between maintenance windows, that only show up for specific data patterns, or that trigger on a mode switch, plus the defects that surface only under relentless repetition with fresh test values.

Neither depth replaces the other, and the numbers show it. The shallow test's 15 days to 70% coverage against the deep test's 6 months makes shallow-and-constant the speed layer. The deep test's 23% unique finds make deep-and-rare the completeness layer. The shallow test's own 7% unique finds close the gap. A fleet running only one regime is choosing between slow detection and permanent blind spots. Meta's recommendation is explicitly both, and the split between them is watched over time as the mix of defect types changes.

Manufactured evidence is the only evidence there will ever be. Injecting known-answer patterns and comparing results turns an invisible failure into an ordinary detection problem, at the permanent cost of running billions of tests a month against machines that are almost always fine. The overhead (4 billion deep-test machine-seconds over the program's life; ~100 million colocated seconds a month) is what "no trace in any log" costs to live with: you pay for constant certainty about the innocent majority in order to catch the silent few.

patterns.note: When a failure leaves no signal to observe, you detect it by asking questions whose answers you already know: inject a known input, check for the known output, and treat any disagreement as the detection. This article shows the pattern deployed at two depths, and the point is that you need both. A shallow, constant version runs beside live workloads (milliseconds, always on) to find most defects fast; a deep, occasional version runs during maintenance (minutes, intrusive) to find the ones nothing else catches. Meta's coverage numbers are the evidence that neither depth substitutes for the other.

Both testing regimes are built to stay out of the way of the work they run beside. Each carries fine controls over how often, how long, and on what hardware a test runs, so that testing a fleet billions of times over does not disturb the workloads it is meant to protect. The other gray-failure articles here (Slack's cellular architecture, Cloudflare's byzantine failure) contain the damage a failure causes; this one contains the cost of the detection itself.

artifact.teaser: Plant a defect that computes wrong answers under one data pattern and watch every health check stay green while corrupted results ship downstream. Arm fleetscanner and catch it at the next maintenance window — months of exposure later; arm ripple and catch it in days; then plant the rare-mode defect only the deep test can see, and learn why the fleet needs both hands.
